summary:
The Human Rights Act 2004 is in force in the Australian Capital Territory and is the statutory rights framework the territory's public authorities must operate within. Courts may issue declarations of inconsistency, and section 31 provides that interpreters may consider international law and the judgments of foreign and international courts and tribunals relevant to a human right. A visitor who encounters discriminatory conduct by an ACT police officer, public servant or public facility therefore has a review mechanism written into territory law. The ACT Legislation Register also records uncommenced amendments made by the Human Rights (Housing) Amendment Act 2025.

The ACT operates an explicit self-identification policy for housing trans and gender-diverse prisoners. Strip-searching inside ACT prisons is documented in a 2026 Human Rights Law Centre report produced with the trans-community groups Flat Out and FIGJAM, which records the disproportionate harms of the practice for trans, gender-diverse and Indigenous prisoners.

Conversion practices are a criminal and civil offence in the territory. The Sexuality and Gender Identity Conversion Practices Bill passed the ACT Legislative Assembly on 27 August 2020 and applied from early 2021, carrying up to 12 months' imprisonment or a $24,000 fine, alongside civil penalties that give the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal power to issue orders and order redress. Practices supporting someone undergoing or considering a gender transition are explicitly not banned. The bill was amended before passage after the Association of Christian Schools and the ACT Law Society argued that the definition of conversion practice was too broad and vague.

Gender-affirming care in the ACT is constrained by capacity rather than by prohibition. The ACT government's LGBTIQ+ Health Scoping Study, reported on 16 April 2022, found serious barriers for transgender and gender-diverse Canberrans: a shortage of primary-care professionals including GPs, mental-health supports and paediatric specialists with LGBTIQ+ health understanding, producing excessive wait times, delays from referrals and high costs associated with interstate and international travel. The study called the ACT the only jurisdiction in the country without a comprehensive gender-focused health service, in private practice or through a publicly-funded gender clinic.
tangentialFactors:
The ACT's explicit self-identification prison policy places it alongside New South Wales, Victoria and Tasmania, which run comparable stated policies; Queensland, the Northern Territory and South Australia are recorded as unclear on the point. A national survey reported on 3 July 2020 estimated up to 400 trans and gender-diverse people held in Australian cells, often inappropriately housed and at elevated risk of physical and sexual violence. That figure is a national estimate with no population denominator, so it indicates scale of exposure rather than a rate.

The territory's conversion-practice statute was narrowed in response to domestic opposition before passage, with the Association of Christian Schools and the ACT Law Society contesting the breadth of the definition. The scope of what now counts as a prohibited conversion practice in the ACT is therefore the amended text, not the bill as introduced.
localsOnly:
Residents needing gender-affirming care face documented queueing. As of April 2022, 20 young transgender people were on the waitlist of Canberra's only paediatric endocrinologist, with some patients waiting a year for an appointment, and GP demand rising 20 to 40 per cent a year. The scoping study attributed the shortfall to a lack of primary-care professionals, mental-health supports and paediatric specialists with LGBTIQ+ health understanding, and recorded the cost of interstate and international travel for care that is not available locally.

ACT residents are protected by territory law against conversion practices, with the Civil and Administrative Tribunal able to issue orders and order redress in addition to criminal penalties, and with practices supporting a person undergoing or considering gender transition carved out of the prohibition. Residents also stand under the Human Rights Act 2004 against the conduct of territory public authorities. The Human Rights (Housing) Amendment Act 2025 is recorded on the legislation register as uncommenced, so its housing protections are not yet in operation.
outOfScopeNotes:
No charging or prosecution data for the ACT's conversion-practice offences appears in the sources reviewed; the enforcement record of the prohibition is unresolved.

The sources do not state how often the ACT's self-identification prison policy has been applied, how trans prisoners have been housed in practice, or how frequently trans prisoners in the ACT have been strip-searched. The 2026 strip-searching report is recorded as covering ACT prisons without ACT-specific figures in this inventory.

The health-capacity findings date from the LGBTIQ+ Health Scoping Study reported in April 2022. No later assessment of ACT gender-health capacity appears in the sources, so whether waitlists and specialist shortages have since changed is unresolved.

Whether the Human Rights (Housing) Amendment Act 2025 has since commenced is unresolved; the legislation register entry available here records it as uncommenced.
